svg.text: A planned removal drains before deleting; a lost host fails over and its volume waits for an operator.
Scale-down: storage pool lowered by one
1. mark the highest-ordinal pod draining
it leaves the placement set; the slot table is recomputed
2. hand over every shard it is primary of
and replace it as replica — ordinary rules and pace, no grace
3. decommission its node record
once it is primary and replica of nothing
4. delete the pod and its volume
never before step 3
Outcome: the cluster shrinks without a failover
the same handover runs one pod at a time on upgrade and eviction
Refused up front
a scale-down leaving fewer pods than the replica count,
or fewer failure domains than the slot table needs
Automatic scale-down only under an explicit scaling policy,
and then it is this drain.
Lost host: a failover, not a scale-down
the pod and its local volume go with the host
unannounced: losing it loses nothing, it costs a short pause
node lease lapses; replicas take its shards over
about 14 s; then repair restores each shard's replica count
volume kept; the operator reports the node lost
the StatefulSet cannot reschedule: the volume is bound to the
lost host. The operator never releases it on its own.
host returns
operator acks
same node, journal back
within the re-placement
delay, with its journal;
the same node ID
replace it
decommission node record,
delete the volume claim;
new pod + new volume
= a new node
Outcome: one failover per shard
no operator action needed to stay writable
Why wait: released automatically, a partition longer than a
timeout would discard a journal that was about to come back.
Identity follows the volume, not the pod name: a StatefulSet reuses ordinals, so a name-derived ID would let an empty journal claim the lost node.
